content.title: WHY YOUR {{HEALTHY}} MEALS AREN'T PAYING OFF
facts: **Overcooked broccoli** – Boiling it until mushy drains most of its vitamin C into the water; steam it for 4-5 minutes instead to keep nutrients intact.
**Draining canned tuna fully** – You're pouring out omega-3-rich oil and liquid; use it in the dressing instead of tossing it down the sink.
**Microwaving in the wrong container** – Reheating in certain plastics can leach chemicals into fatty or acidic foods; switch to glass or ceramic.
**Salting meat too early** – Salting right before cooking pulls out moisture and leaves it dry; salt 40 minutes ahead or right at the pan.
**Tossing egg yolks** – Egg-white-only omelets skip most of the choline and vitamin D the egg actually has; the yolk isn't the villain you think it is.
**Peeling vegetables out of habit** – Potato and cucumber skins hold a good chunk of the fiber; a quick scrub beats peeling for most veggies.
**Cooking with the lid off** – Letting steam escape means water-soluble vitamins evaporate faster; a lid traps both heat and nutrients.
**Adding oil to boiling pasta water** – It doesn't stop sticking, it just coats the noodles so sauce slides right off later; a good stir does the real work.

content.caption:
Small cooking habits quietly cancel out the effort you put into eating well. Take broccoli – once it's boiled past that bright green stage, a big chunk of its vitamin C has already leached into the cooking water, so steaming or a quick stir-fry protects far more of it. The same goes for egg yolks: skipping them to "save calories" also means skipping choline, which your brain and liver actually rely on daily, and most of the vitamin D the egg provides. And with vegetables like potatoes or cucumbers, peeling out of habit strips away fiber sitting just under the skin that helps slow digestion and keep you full longer. Everyone's kitchen shortcuts are different, so it's worth noticing which ones you actually do.
